parts.passage:
Learning to Swim as an Adult

Last summer, I finally decided to learn how to swim properly. I had avoided lessons for years, mainly because I felt embarrassed about starting so late. (12) Still, I told myself that it was better to try than to keep avoiding the water forever.

The first lesson was more difficult than I expected. My instructor asked me to float on my back, something I had never managed before. (13) Every time I tried, I tensed up and sank almost immediately.

By the third week, however, something began to change. I could float for a few seconds without panicking, and my confidence slowly grew. (14) My instructor said this was completely normal and encouraged me to keep practising.

As the weeks went by, I started swimming short distances across the pool. (15) Friends who already knew how to swim seemed surprised at how quickly I was improving.

Eventually, I signed up for a longer course that included open water sessions at a nearby lake. (16) The water felt colder and less predictable than the swimming pool, and at first this made me nervous.

Looking back now, I am glad that I did not give up after that first lesson. (17) I now swim regularly, and I even encourage other adults who are hesitant to give it a try.
options: A) It seemed like a strange skill to be missing at my age.
B) Progress, however, was not always steady.
C) I also began to enjoy the exercise more than I had anticipated.
D) It was a completely different experience from swimming indoors.
E) At times, I wondered whether I would ever manage it at all.
F) Learning as an adult has taught me patience as much as swimming itself.
G) Most beginners give up within the first few sessions.

A
When the community garden opened, few people expected it to attract much interest. Today, more than eighty households are on the waiting list, and additional plots are being cleared to meet demand. While members are pleased with its popularity, several have complained that securing a plot now takes over a year.

B
The choir welcomes new singers by pairing them with more experienced members during their first few rehearsals. Organisers say this approach helps newcomers feel comfortable more quickly and makes them more likely to stay involved long-term. A number of former newcomers now act as mentors themselves.

C
For many years, the family who run the restaurant refused to offer a delivery service, worried that it might affect the quality of the food or the atmosphere of the dining room. They eventually changed their minds during a quiet period, and the decision is now seen as one that saved the business.

The pop-up cinema is known for showing a different, often unusual selection of films every month, with the exact programme kept secret until the night itself. Regular visitors say that not knowing what they will see is part of the enjoyment, and attendance is highest when the theme is most unpredictable.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.instructions: Read the article and answer the questions.
parts.passage:
The Shift Towards Shorter Working Weeks

For most of the last century, a five-day working week was considered standard practice across much of the developed world. Employees were expected to work broadly similar hours from Monday to Friday, with the idea of a shorter working week largely confined to occasional debate rather than serious policy. However, this arrangement is increasingly being questioned by employers, employees and researchers alike.

In recent years, a growing number of companies have experimented with a four-day working week, usually maintaining full pay while reducing total hours. Advocates argue that a shorter week can lead to a more focused and motivated workforce, particularly in roles that involve a high degree of concentration or creativity. Rather than measuring value purely by hours spent at a desk, supporters suggest that output and results should matter more.

One frequently cited advantage is the potential improvement in employee wellbeing. Trials in several countries have reported that staff experience lower levels of stress and improved work-life balance when given an additional day off each week. Some employees have used the extra time to spend with family, pursue hobbies or simply rest, which in turn appears to reduce burnout and staff turnover.

Productivity is another area of interest. Contrary to what many assumed, several organisations that adopted a four-day week did not see an overall drop in output. Instead, some reported that employees became more efficient during the days they did work, cutting down on unnecessary meetings and minimising distractions in order to complete tasks within a shorter timeframe.

Nonetheless, the model is not without its critics. Certain industries, particularly those involving shift work, healthcare or customer-facing roles, argue that reducing working days is far more difficult to implement without increasing costs or affecting service levels. Smaller businesses in particular may struggle to maintain the same level of output without hiring additional staff, which is not always financially realistic.

There are also concerns about how a shorter week might affect long-term career expectations. Some critics worry that employees working fewer days could be seen as less committed, potentially affecting promotion opportunities, regardless of their actual performance during working hours.

Despite these challenges, interest in alternative working patterns continues to grow. Many analysts believe that as technology continues to automate routine tasks, the traditional link between hours worked and value produced will become increasingly outdated. While a universal shift to a four-day week remains unlikely in the near future, flexible approaches to working time are expected to become more common across a wider range of industries.
